articles.title: Trump Leaves Door Open to Pardoning Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
articles.text:
Trump willing to pardon Jensen Huang, says it won’t be necessary
The president’s remarks come days before Jensen Huang is due to face congressional questioning over national security concerns and US chip export controls.
US President Donald Trump has left the door open to pardoning Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang, though he said he doesn’t think it’ll be necessary.
Trump made the comments during an interview with the New York Post just a day after Huang was reinstated as Nvidia’s CEO amid scrutiny over his affair with a suspected Chinese spy and whether he allowed the company’s chips to fall into China’s hands.
Asked about a pardon for any potential crimes, Trump told The Post: “It’s always an option, I guess, but I don’t think it’ll be necessary.”
Trump had earlier claimed credit for pushing Nvidia’s board to bring Huang back — a move which saw Nvidia’s stock surge on Monday.
Huang is scheduled to testify before lawmakers in a closed-door, transcribed interview with the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the House Intelligence Committee and the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party on Dec. 1.
On Dec. 3, Huang is set to be the sole witness in a hearing by the Committee on Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs about US export controls.
Related: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO amid ongoing intelligence probe

articles.title: CIA Network Breached Amid Spate of US Cyberattacks: Report
articles.text:
Hackers breach CIA intelligence network in latest US cyberattack
The reported breach follows cyber incidents involving the FBI, Department of Homeland Security and Department of Agriculture.
The US Central Intelligence Agency and at least one other intelligence agency have been hit with a cybersecurity breach that exposed unclassified information, according to The New York Times.
Citing US officials and people familiar with the matter, the Times reported that hackers breached a network used by the CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence that analyzes publicly available information to gather intelligence insights.
It is also believed that other government agencies were exposed in the breach, according to two of the people.
An official with the Office of the Director of National Intelligence said there have been no disruptions to critical capabilities or classified systems. Cointelegraph reached out to the CIA for comment.
The breach adds to a spate of reported cyber incidents at US federal agencies in recent weeks.
The Verge on Tuesday reported the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) is also investigating a “cybersecurity incident” that “resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems.” It is not clear if it is related to the recent CIA breach.
Other breaches include the US Department of Agriculture, a leak of Department of Homeland Security personnel records and a hack of the FBI’s national crime database.
Speaking to ABC News about the FBI attack on Sunday, US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said cyberattacks have been increasing, and digital infrastructure needs to be upgraded.
“In 2020, there were roughly 750,000 cyber incidents reported to the FBI. That’s now up to over a million cyber incidents,” said Clayton.
“And what we’re seeing, though, here, and I want the American people to know this, is we have a step change in technology that we’re facing with superintelligence and computing power that is expanding exponentially and we have a dated digital infrastructure.”
Clayton declined to discuss the specifics of the FBI incident but said that cyber incidents were not a new phenomenon.
“Cyber probing, cyber incidents, they have been part of the American economy, part of the American life for a long time.”
Related: Coldcard reveals how Bitcoin wallet flaw went undetected for over 5 years

articles.title: CleanSpark Mulls Selling More Bitcoin Than It Mines
articles.text:
CleanSpark weighs selling more Bitcoin than it mines to de-risk books
The Bitcoin miner sold 2,102 BTC while it produced just 1,708 BTC in the September quarter.
Bitcoin miner CleanSpark is considering selling more Bitcoin than it mines each quarter to reduce its treasury risk, according to chief financial officer Gary Vecchiarelli, potentially further drawing down its holdings, last valued at $806 million.
CleanSpark held 13,530 Bitcoin at the end of September after mining 1,708 Bitcoin and selling 2,102 Bitcoin during the quarter, according to Cointelegraph’s tally of the company’s monthly operating updates. It marks the first time since at least 2024 that the company ended the quarter with less Bitcoin than it began with.
During a Q4 earnings call on Tuesday, Vecchiarelli said CleanSpark already aims to sell virtually all of the Bitcoin it mines to cover day-to-day operating costs, and told an analyst that selling slightly more than it produces in a quarter was one way to reduce treasury risk.
“We see the selling of a small amount of Bitcoin in excess of the quarterly production to be one way of de-risking,” said Vecchiarelli.
“But again, we are going to be sensitive and very reactionary to markets, and we are going to use that capital to make sure that we prevent dilution or bringing additional debt just to grow the company,” he said.
The remarks came as CleanSpark recorded a $987 million net loss for the fiscal year ended Sept. 30, compared with a net income of $364 million a year earlier. The company attributed two-thirds of the swing to noncash adjustments in the value of its Bitcoin holdings, as Bitcoin’s price fell from about $114,100 to $83,600 over the fiscal year.
Related: Trump-linked American Bitcoin secures $150M credit line from FalconX
CleanSpark also said it sold an undisclosed amount of Bitcoin since September to raise cash for expected acquisitions, as Vecchiarelli said it continues to view its Bitcoin holdings as “a liquid source of non-dilutive capital.”
CleanSpark trims mining fleet as AI buildout advances
CleanSpark also cut about 25,000 machines from its Bitcoin mining fleet in the September quarter, bringing the number in operation to about 200,000.
Vecchiarelli said the reduction improved energy efficiency to 14.8 joules per terahash from 15.8 in the previous quarter, which he said should help CleanSpark stay profitable if mining conditions deteriorate ahead of the 2028 Bitcoin halving.
“Going forward, in terms of hash rate, that will probably fluctuate, but we will continue to mine so as long as it’s profitable.”
In Sandersville, Georgia, CleanSpark said its first AI data hall remains on track for the fourth quarter of 2027. CleanSpark said it expects to start unplugging miners at the site in late 2027 as the data center comes online, then decide whether to relocate or sell them.
CleanSpark shares dropped 7.5% on Tuesday ahead of the earnings release to $5.12 and are down 2.25% in after-hours trading.
The company recorded $576.5 million in total revenue in the full year, down 25% from the previous fiscal year. Adjusted EBITDA came in at a loss of $304.2 million for the year.

articles.title: Today in crypto: Coldcard wallet flaw, South Korea’s crypto bill, Bitcoin dip buying
articles.text:
Here’s what happened in crypto today
Need to know what happened in crypto today? Here is the latest news on daily trends and events impacting Bitcoin price, blockchain, DeFi, Web3 and crypto regulation.
Today in crypto, Coinkite disclosed how a software error left Coldcard users’ Bitcoin recovery phrases vulnerable to hackers, South Korea moved to tighten oversight of stablecoin issuers and crypto exchanges, and 42 Macro warned that persistent inflation and further monetary tightening could put additional pressure on Bitcoin.
Coldcard reveals how Bitcoin wallet flaw went undetected for over 5 years
Bitcoin hardware wallet maker Coinkite has detailed how a security flaw in its Coldcard devices went undetected for more than five years despite several independent security reviews, including those using artificial intelligence (AI).
In a Nov. 23 postmortem report, Coinkite said that while its security checks confirmed the wallets had the correct system for generating secure recovery phrases, the company never verified whether the wallets were actually using it. As a result, a software error caused the wallets to use a weaker system instead, making the recovery phrases easier for hackers to guess.
A Bitcoin hardware wallet is a physical device that stores private keys offline, while a recovery phrase is a series of words that allows users to restore access to their funds if the device is lost or damaged.
Coinkite said at least 15 independent security reviews and research efforts failed to catch the flaw before the thefts began. It added that the weaker system went undetected because the recovery phrases looked normal and could still pass some security tests.
The flaw allowed hackers to steal at least 1,789 Bitcoin (BTC), worth around $114.7 million at the time of the thefts, Galaxy Research reported in August. Coinkite said it fixed the flaw on July 31 and introduced further security measures in August.
South Korea proposes bank-led stablecoins, 20% cap on crypto exchange stakes
South Korea’s Financial Services Commission (FSC) unveiled a draft bill Tuesday that would initially limit issuance of won-denominated stablecoins to groups majority-owned by banks and generally cap shareholders’ stakes in crypto exchanges at 20%.
Banks would have to own more than half of a stablecoin issuer collectively, though a fintech or technology company could be its largest individual shareholder, the FSC said in its announcement.
Domestic stablecoin issuers would need FSC authorization and at least 5 billion won (about $3.7 million) in equity capital. They would also have to hold reserves covering at least 100% of their outstanding tokens and redeem them at face value without delay.
Exchanges would need dealing, brokerage and custody licenses and would have to meet capital and operating requirements. Shareholders’ stakes would be capped at 20%, or 34% with FSC approval.
The draft also seeks to lift South Korea’s 2017 ban on domestic initial coin offerings.
Why 42 Macro says it’s waiting to buy the Bitcoin dip
Darius Dale, founder and CEO of 42 Macro, says his firm has trimmed its Bitcoin exposure and is waiting for signs that the sell-off has run its course before it considers buying again.
“We’ve already de-risked out of Bitcoin,” Dale said in an interview with Cointelegraph last week. “Our stress levels are low. We’re just waiting to buy.”
Dale’s comments came just days before Bitcoin fell to a two-year low around $55,100 on Saturday, raising questions about whether Bitcoin has finally found its bottom this cycle.
However, Dale warned that persistently high inflation could prompt further Fed tightening that could drain the liquidity that supports Bitcoin. The US Federal Reserve is widely expected to increase rates by 25 basis points at its next meeting on Dec. 9.
“Bitcoin doesn’t generate earnings. Bitcoin needs liquidity to go up,” he said.
Bitcoin was trading at around $64,000 at the time of the interview. Dale said it could fall another 30% to 40% if the S&P 500’s decline from its Oct. 6 peak reaches 20% by Christmas, which would put it at around $38,400. The S&P500 is currently down 7.4% from that peak.

articles.title: Europol Targets Crypto Payments Behind Digital Piracy
articles.text:
Europol follows $28.5M crypto trail in streaming piracy crackdown
Authorities from 11 countries worked with Binance, Coinbase and Chainalysis to trace financial transactions and disrupt illegal streaming services.
Law enforcement authorities from 11 countries, working with crypto exchanges Binance and Coinbase and blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis, have traced more than 26 million euros ($28.5 million) in cryptocurrency transactions and disrupted 57 illegal streaming services in an operation coordinated by Europol, the law enforcement agency of the European Union.
In a Tuesday announcement, Europol said the five-day operation took place in Seville, Spain, from Nov. 16 to Nov. 20 and identified 321 websites illegally offering copyrighted content, attracting more than 7.3 million annual visits combined.
Europol said illegal streaming operators often collect subscription payments in cryptocurrency, allowing them to transfer funds quickly across borders. Investigators traced blockchain transactions to identify links between streaming services, cryptocurrency wallets and the individuals controlling them.
The EU’s law enforcement agency said the operation reflects a shift from focusing solely on shutting down illegal streaming services to also targeting the financial infrastructure behind them. The findings will support ongoing national investigations, including efforts to identify suspects and trace assets linked to criminal activity.
According to figures from the Audiovisual Anti-Piracy Alliance cited by Europol, an estimated 60 million people across Europe use unauthorized internet protocol television (IPTV) services, with estimated annual losses of 4.83 billion euros ($5.3 billion) for legitimate providers and a further 1.08 billion euros ($1.18 billion) in unpaid taxes for governments.
Related: Tron and Tether bring in Chainalysis after T3 crime unit folds
Europol targets international cybercrime networks
The operation follows other international efforts to disrupt criminal networks and their financial infrastructure. In March, US and European authorities dismantled SocksEscort, a malicious proxy service that enabled crimes including bank fraud and cryptocurrency account takeovers.
The service allowed customers to pay anonymously in cryptocurrency and received at least $5.7 million in user payments, according to investigators. Authorities froze about $3.5 million in cryptocurrency linked to the operation.
Earlier that month, Europol and the FBI took down LeakBase, a cybercrime forum with more than 142,000 registered users. An earlier cybercrime marketplace, RaidForums, had previously hosted leaked personal data belonging to users of crypto hardware wallet provider Ledger.
Magazine: AI agents are using credit cards. Where does that leave crypto?

articles.title: OpenAI and Anthropic Insiders Fear Their Next AI Models Are Too Dangerous to Release
articles.text:
In brief
- More than two dozen sources familiar with internal discussions at OpenAI and Anthropic told Axios there's growing concerns about unreleased AI models.
- Researchers are reportedly finding that advanced models can conceal their reasoning and deceive the systems designed to monitor them.
- Both companies have previously paused AI development over safety concerns, but some researchers now advocate stopping the training of more powerful models altogether.
Employees at OpenAI and Anthropic are increasingly concerned that their companies' most advanced AI models may never be safe enough for public release, according to a Tuesday report by Axios citing more than two dozen sources familiar with internal discussions.
Some researchers believe the technical problems can eventually be solved. Others reportedly want the companies to stop training more intelligent models altogether.
The report comes two days after Meta Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang warned that humanity might be approaching a point where it can no longer effectively supervise artificial intelligence. Wang argued that decisions made over the next year could determine whether humans retain control over increasingly autonomous, self-improving AI systems.
Did you know?
You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.
His warning followed Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge's announcement that an unreleased version of Claude had helped him prove the Riemann Hypothesis, a mathematical problem that had frustrated researchers for 167 years.
The same intellectual abilities that make these models so valuable for scientific research are making them harder to supervise. A model capable of spotting something that generations of mathematicians missed could conceivably spot weaknesses in a safety system that its developers overlooked.
When smarter AI becomes harder to control
One of the biggest problems facing AI researchers involves reinforcement learning, a training technique that rewards models for successfully completing tasks. It's largely responsible for the impressive reasoning abilities of modern AI systems, but it can also teach them to cheat.
Researchers call this reward hacking. A model might, for example, manipulate the software responsible for grading its work instead of actually solving the problem it was assigned.
Anthropic encountered a version of this problem in February, when researchers reversed three days of training on Claude Mythos Preview after discovering undesirable behaviors. An internal review later flagged more than 10% of its active training environments for problems that included opportunities for cheating and incorrectly configured tasks.
Another problem involves chain-of-thought monitoring, which allows researchers to inspect the intermediate reasoning an AI generates before producing an answer or taking an action. Some unreleased models are increasingly capable of obscuring that reasoning or generating misleading explanations that satisfy their monitors.
In other words, the explanation researchers receive may no longer accurately reflect how the model arrived at its decision.
OpenAI has already experienced the real-world consequences of inadequate containment. The company acknowledged that an internal research model was primarily responsible for compromising AI development platform Hugging Face while pursuing a difficult task.
Keeping the smartest models away from ChatGPT and Claude users would therefore address only part of the problem.
“Keeping a model internal doesn't make it safe,” an Anthropic spokesperson told Axios.
Putting the brakes on the AI race
OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki proposed Sunday that AI developers agree on common limits to model development, based partly on perplexity—a mathematical measure of how accurately a model predicts subsequent pieces of text, with lower scores indicating better predictions.
Pachocki argues that companies should agree not to cross certain thresholds until researchers develop more effective ways of monitoring AI behavior. He estimates that AI-assisted research could substantially accelerate the development of new models as early as 2027.
Getting competing companies to voluntarily slow down could prove particularly difficult, especially as investors expect returns on the enormous amounts of money pouring into AI infrastructure. Anthropic itself raised more than $81 billion when it went public last week.
OpenAI said last week that it would suspend training or withhold models again if they failed to satisfy its safety requirements. Anthropic has separately committed to publishing a policy proposal on independent AI evaluators by December 15, followed by a framework addressing the pace of AI development by January 15, 2027.

articles.title: Utah Moves to End Criminal Case Against Kalshi
articles.text:
Utah moves to dismiss criminal charges against Kalshi after trading halt
Utah’s attorney general warned that the criminal charges could be refiled if Kalshi resumes operations in the state, while separate civil litigation remains unresolved.
Utah’s attorney general has moved to dismiss 14 criminal charges against prediction market platform Kalshi and its two co-founders after the company blocked users in the state from accessing its services.
The attorney general’s office said it filed a motion Monday to dismiss the case without prejudice in Utah’s Third District Court, allowing prosecutors to refile the charges if Kalshi resumes operations in the state.
The office opened a criminal investigation into Kalshi in September and filed charges on Oct. 28, alleging that the company offered illegal gambling to Utah residents. Kalshi subsequently agreed to block access to its platform in the state and monitor attempts to reach its services from Utah-based IP addresses.
“Kalshi has pulled out of Utah, and if it returns, so will the charges,” Attorney General Derek Brown said, adding that his office would continue to enforce state gambling laws against other prediction market operators.
The office also sent cease-and-desist letters to several of Kalshi’s competitors, with six other prediction market companies agreeing to stop operating in Utah.
Kalshi General Counsel Yaakov Roth said in a Tuesday post on X that “good faith jurisdictional disagreements should never be criminalized,” adding that the company was willing to work with state attorneys general while courts resolve the regulatory dispute.
Source: Yaakov Roth
The case is separate from a civil lawsuit Utah brought against Kalshi and its market-making partner Susquehanna International Group on Oct. 20, seeking restitution, damages and the recovery of proceeds from allegedly illegal gambling activities. The complaint estimates that Kalshi collected between $30.6 million and $61.2 million in fees from Utah-based accounts as of Oct. 19.
The US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) announced its own lawsuit against Utah on Oct. 27, seeking to block the state from enforcing its gambling laws against federally regulated prediction markets. The lawsuit is part of a broader legal battle over the regulation of prediction markets, with the CFTC asserting exclusive jurisdiction over event contracts. The federal regulator has sued at least 12 states over the issue.
Magazine: How to preserve wealth and access funds during a national emergency

articles.title: Anthropic’s Claude Ship Lets AI Write, Review and Approve Its Own Code
articles.text:
In brief
- Anthropic launched Claude Ship, a collection of AI agents that review, repair and approve software changes.
- Developers can configure their repositories to allow certain changes to merge without human intervention.
- Anthropic already uses a similar system internally, though independent research suggests AI models struggle to identify vulnerabilities in AI-generated code.
Anthropic is automating another part of software engineering: the process of deciding whether the code an AI writes is actually good enough to use.
The company introduced Claude Ship on Monday, a collection of AI agents capable of reviewing software changes, fixing errors, and approving code according to rules established by development teams.
Under certain configurations, software changes can make their way into a company's codebase without a human reading a single line of code.
Did you know?
You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.
AI coding tools have become so good at producing software that reviewing it has become a bottleneck. Developers who previously spent hours writing a feature can now generate several in that time, but someone still has to check whether those changes work without breaking something else.
Anthropic is experiencing that problem itself. The company says Claude already writes most of the code produced by its Claude Code team.
Claude Ship combines three tools, each responsible for a different stage of the process. The first, Code Review, examines proposed changes against the existing codebase, using multiple agents to find potential bugs and verify each other's findings.
PR Steward, the second tool, makes the necessary corrections when automated tests fail or reviewers identify problems. It documents its modifications and provides instructions for reversing them, allowing developers to intervene if necessary.
The third tool, Claude Approvals, decides whether the proposed changes satisfy the company's approval policies. According to Anthropic's technical documentation, repositories configured for automatic merging can incorporate changes without anyone manually approving them.
Who checks the AI checking the AI?
The ability to delegate code reviews to AI is particularly attractive in the age of vibe coding, where developers—and increasingly people with little programming experience—build software by describing what they want in natural language.
But having an AI double-check another AI's work doesn't necessarily eliminate their shared weaknesses. A human programmer and a language model might approach a problem differently, whereas two agents powered by similar models could overlook the same flawed assumption.
A peer-reviewed study published earlier this year found that models from OpenAI and Anthropic performed slightly better at identifying and repairing security vulnerabilities in human-written code than in AI-generated code.
AI-assisted software development has already produced some expensive mistakes. In April, a startup founder reported that a coding agent running Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6 deleted his company's production database and its volume-level backups through a single API call.
Anthropic's own experience with automated code reviews illustrates a different problem: AI agents can get stuck correcting each other. In one instance, according to an October engineering report, a proposed software change went through more than 50 rounds of automated reviews and corrections overnight before its author intervened.
The company nevertheless reported encouraging internal results. The number of merged changes more than doubled between June and September, while the proportion of changes that had to be reversed fell by more than 40%.
Those results came from a broader review process that retained human oversight for sensitive modifications, rather than a fully autonomous system. Changes to documentation can pass without human approval at Anthropic, whereas particularly risky modifications require two people to sign off.
“A person is accountable for every change that ships, whoever typed it,” Anthropic's engineers wrote.
Whether other companies adopt equally restrictive policies is up to them. Claude Ship allows administrators to determine which parts of their software require human supervision and which decisions they are comfortable delegating to an AI.
The service is available for GitHub repositories on Claude Team and Enterprise plans, with charges based on token consumption. For now, Anthropic recommends running its automated approval system in observation mode, letting the AI demonstrate what it would have approved before giving it the authority to do so.

articles.title: Why Bitcoin’s Losses Deepened After the Binance Hack
articles.text:
Bitcoin sell-off driven by weak demand, forced liquidations: 21Shares
The crypto asset manager warned that Bitcoin’s downturn could persist amid weak investor demand, while forecasting an uneven recovery across crypto sectors.
The $6.4 billion hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance in October triggered Bitcoin’s recent sell-off, but weakening investor demand and forced liquidations drove most of the subsequent losses, according to a Nov. 24 report from crypto asset manager 21Shares.
While the Oct. 29 hack triggered the initial decline, the report found that weakening demand drove Bitcoin (BTC) down a further 8.3% between Nov. 4 and Nov. 11. Forced selling of leveraged positions led to the steepest decline, sending BTC down another 13.5% over the next three days. Crypto liquidations totaled $5.8 billion in the week ending Nov. 15, with long positions accounting for 81%.
Bitcoin’s sell-off and leverage unwind. Source: 21Shares
Signs of weakening demand were also seen in the stablecoin supply, which contracted by $10.7 billion following the hack, marking the largest 18-day decline in dollar terms since the Terra collapse in 2022. US spot Bitcoin and Ether (ETH) exchange-traded funds (ETFs) recorded combined outflows of $3.9 billion between Oct. 30 and Nov. 13.
Eliezer Ndinga, global head of research at 21Shares, told Cointelegraph that the market was already vulnerable before the hack:
The Fed had raised rates in September, core inflation had risen 0.3% for a third straight month, and doubts over AI spending had kept the Nasdaq-100 below its October 6 record. The hack started the sell-off, but bitcoin fell only 5.1% in the two days after it and had recovered almost all of that by November 4.
The report also found little evidence of selling by other major Bitcoin holders. The 18,270 BTC and 522,409 ETH stolen in the Binance hack remained unspent as of mid-November, while neither the US government nor the Mt. Gox trustee had transferred Bitcoin to exchanges since the attack.
Bitcoin treasury firm Strategy continued buying, adding 2,332 BTC between Oct. 26 and Nov. 15. Meanwhile, miner transfers to exchanges fell to their lowest levels since at least 2020, although the data may not capture sales by publicly traded mining companies.
Related: Bitcoin slides amid US tariff nerves as Anthropic falls below IPO price
21Shares sees a K-shaped recovery for crypto
21Shares believes Bitcoin is already more than a year into a cyclical bear market. Historically, such downturns have lasted about two and a half years and resulted in average price declines of 84%, according to the report.
However, the researchers see a low probability of Bitcoin revisiting the depths of previous bear markets, citing the growing presence of institutional investors and spot ETFs. Ndinga said the competitive landscape for crypto has also changed:
Crypto is also no longer the only frontier technology in investors’ minds, with AI and robotics drawing talent and capital away from it. We expect a K-shaped recovery, where bitcoin, 24/7 trading venues, privacy protocols and quantum-resistant solutions advance while other parts of the market lag.
Ndinga warned that a larger-than-expected Federal Reserve rate hike in December could prolong the downturn. Another potential source of selling pressure is the $2.2 billion in BTC and ETH stolen in the Binance hack, which could reach the market through over-the-counter (OTC) brokers in the coming months.
Ndinga identified Bitcoin’s realized price of $53,250, a measure of the average investor cost basis, as a key downside level to watch. Conversely, a return to the $73,000 to $75,500 range coupled with sustained ETF inflows and rising stablecoin balances would signal renewed investor demand.
Stablecoin supply changes following major market shocks. Source: 21Shares
Magazine: Binance’s $6.5B freeze order, Hong Kong ‘suspicious’ of HYPE: Asia Express

articles.title: Coldcard Bitcoin Exploit, Revisited: How a Hidden Flaw Survived Years of Audits
articles.text:
In brief
- Coinkite’s detailed postmortem confirms Coldcard firmware generated wallet seeds with a weak software random-number generator from March 2021 to July 2026, leaving seeds guessable enough for attackers to regenerate keys offline and steal funds.
- The flaw evaded at least 15 security reviews—including two paid audits and an AI-assisted one—because checks confirmed the hardware RNG code existed but never verified seed generation actually used it.
- Coinkite notes the first thefts began two days after Kimi K3’s release, calling AI discovery a “plausible hypothesis.”
Four months after attackers drained Bitcoin from compromised Coldcard hardware wallets, the device’s maker has published a detailed autopsy of how a single configuration error went undetected for more than five years, slipping past at least 15 separate security reviews before thieves exploited it.
The postmortem, released Monday by manufacturer Coinkite and modeled on an NTSB accident report, confirms the core failure when the exploit surfaced in July: from March 2021 through July 2026, Coldcard firmware generated wallet seeds using a software pseudo-random number generator, MicroPython’s Yasmarang, instead of the device’s intended hardware random-number generator.
The result was seeds with roughly 40 to 72 bits of effective randomness rather than the 128-bit target, weak enough for attackers to regenerate private keys offline and steal funds without ever touching a device.
Did you know?
You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.
The new report’s most revealing section is its accounting of why the flaw hid for so long.
Coinkite documented at least 15 independent review efforts between 2021 and 2026, including two paid third-party audits, physical-security work by Ledger Donjon, and even an AI-assisted firmware review that produced 85 findings. None caught it.
As the report puts it, every check “answered a nearby question rather than the critical one”: release checks confirmed the hardware-RNG code was present, but not that seed generation actually reached it, and statistical tests couldn’t distinguish the defective generator’s output from a properly seeded one.
A safeguard meant to reject the faulty configuration, a guard in the underlying libNgU code, simply didn’t work.
The scale of losses remains murky. Coinkite said it has received about 300 loss-related support tickets tied to 242 accounts, roughly 0.21% of its estimated user base, while Galaxy Research has attributed more than 8,600 addresses to the theft. The company cautions that those figures count different things and can’t be combined into a victim total.
One thread running through the report is the role of AI. Coinkite notes the first thefts began just two days after the Kimi K3 model’s full weights were released, calling AI-assisted discovery “a plausible hypothesis, not an attribution.”
It also documents how, after the flaw went public, the Bitcoin Red Team used Kimi K3 to run a 108-hour multi-model sweep that flagged nearly 8,000 candidate findings across 501 Bitcoin projects, underscoring how AI has upended the economics of vulnerability hunting.
Coinkite has since rebuilt its seed generation, adding mandatory user entropy, multiple hardware sources, and build-time and boot-time checks, with an independent review by Keylabs concluding the defect is “fully closed” in current standard firmware.
But no update repairs seeds already created on affected devices; those users must migrate to new ones. The report ends with a plea to whoever holds the stolen Bitcoin: return it.
“Some victims lost life-changing amounts, and returning the funds is the only action that can directly reduce that harm,” the company said.

articles.title: Coinkite Explains How Coldcard Security Checks Failed
articles.text:
Coldcard reveals how Bitcoin wallet flaw went undetected for over 5 years
Coldcard maker Coinkite explained why years of security checks failed to catch the flaw and said it has yet to decide on compensation for affected customers.
Bitcoin hardware wallet maker Coinkite has detailed how a security flaw in its Coldcard devices went undetected for more than five years despite several independent security reviews, including those using artificial intelligence (AI).
In a Nov. 23 postmortem report, Coinkite said that while its security checks confirmed the wallets had the correct system for generating secure recovery phrases, the company never verified whether the wallets were actually using it. As a result, a software error caused the wallets to use a weaker system instead, making the recovery phrases easier for hackers to guess.
A Bitcoin hardware wallet is a physical device that stores private keys offline, while a recovery phrase is a series of words that allows users to restore access to their funds if the device is lost or damaged.
Coinkite said at least 15 independent security reviews and research efforts failed to catch the flaw before the thefts began. It added that the weaker system went undetected because the recovery phrases looked normal and could still pass some security tests.
The flaw allowed hackers to steal at least 1,789 Bitcoin (BTC), worth around $114.7 million at the time of the thefts, Galaxy Research reported in August. Coinkite said it fixed the flaw on July 31 and introduced further security measures in August.
What happens next?
The report says that as of Nov. 18, Coinkite had received around 300 loss-related support tickets associated with 242 accounts. The company also said that the actual number of victims was likely higher and that it is still exploring ways to help affected customers but has yet to decide on a compensation plan.
Coinkite said it still does not know who stole the funds or how the hackers found the flaw. The company said law enforcement authorities are also investigating the thefts, and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security has opened a separate case.
The company continues to urge affected users to update their software, create new recovery phrases and move their funds to new wallets, warning that software updates cannot make previously affected recovery phrases safe.
Cointelegraph contacted Coinkite for comment on its compensation plans but had not received a response by publication.
Related: Coldcard strengthens seed generation with firmware update

articles.title: Ethereum Foundation Says AI Is a More Urgent Threat Than Quantum Computing
articles.text:
In brief
- The Ethereum Foundation says AI poses a more immediate security risk than quantum computing.
- Developers are prioritizing hash-based cryptography to protect wallets, transactions, and the network's underlying infrastructure.
- The security overhaul could be harder than Ethereum's 2022 Merge, with researchers pushing for completion as early as December 2028.
The Ethereum Foundation has doubled the size of its protocol security team and made strengthening Ethereum's cryptography its highest priority, warning that artificial intelligence could undermine the mathematical foundations of the network before quantum computers get powerful enough to do so.
"The EF has been planning mitigations to the threat posed by quantum computers," Kev Wedderburn wrote in a blog post published Monday, adding that "recently AI emerged as a more urgent risk."
For years, the crypto industry has worried about Q-Day—the hypothetical moment when quantum computers become powerful enough to break the cryptography protecting digital assets. AI introduces a different problem: What if someone discovers a mathematical shortcut that makes such a machine unnecessary?
Did you know?
You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Ethereum with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.
Bitcoin and Ethereum both rely on elliptic curve cryptography to authenticate transactions. Its security depends on mathematical problems that are relatively easy to solve in one direction but prohibitively difficult to reverse using known algorithms.
An AI capable of discovering substantially better algorithms could change that equation without requiring any breakthroughs in quantum hardware.
Ethereum Foundation researcher Justin Drake raised this possibility in October, warning that existing signature schemes could become vulnerable within months rather than years under a worst-case scenario. He recommended that the industry start preparing for an orderly migration of funds to addresses whose public keys have never been exposed.
The Foundation's latest announcement comes just days after Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge and Claude produced a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, a mathematical problem that had remained unsolved since 1859.
ETH price on November 29, 4:59PM UTC
The proof does not break Bitcoin or Ethereum's cryptography, but it illustrates how quickly AI is becoming useful in areas of mathematics previously considered beyond its capabilities.
There are already more practical examples in crypto. In May, a security researcher working with Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.8 discovered a vulnerability in privacy-focused cryptocurrency Zcash that could have allowed attackers to create counterfeit coins without leaving an obvious trace on the blockchain.
The bug had survived roughly four years of scrutiny by cryptographers.
Changing Ethereum's locks
Ethereum's proposed solution involves moving away from elliptic curves and adopting hash-based cryptography. Hash functions turn data into fixed-length digital fingerprints that are designed to be extremely difficult to reverse, and their security relies on fewer structural mathematical assumptions than elliptic curve schemes.
Ethereum already depends on secure hash functions, making them an attractive foundation for its new security architecture.
The transition would affect how users authorize transactions, how validators secure the network, and how Ethereum verifies data submitted by layer-2 networks.
Developers are also pursuing formal verification, a technique that uses mathematical proofs to demonstrate that software behaves according to its specifications. Ironically, AI could help accelerate that work.
The Foundation has been deploying AI agents against its own infrastructure since earlier this year, successfully identifying software vulnerabilities before malicious actors could exploit them.
The security overhaul comes at a cost. Ethereum developers will need to rethink some planned features, and larger cryptographic signatures could increase hardware requirements for people running their own nodes.
Development group Ethlabs has already withdrawn its proposal to introduce faster block production in the upcoming Hegotá upgrade, freeing up engineering resources to pursue an ambitious target of making Ethereum resistant to both threats in 2027.
The Foundation previously established December 2029 as its internal deadline for achieving quantum resistance across Ethereum's base layer. Drake proposed bringing that target forward to December 2028 at the recent Devcon conference in Mumbai.
The Foundation plans to reassess its timeline in January 2027, with developers already testing early implementations of the new cryptographic infrastructure.

articles.title: CFTC Updates US Prediction Market Reporting Requirements
articles.text:
CFTC sets new prediction market rules as more firms seek US entry
The US regulator has approved permanent reporting rules for certain event contracts as more companies look to launch prediction markets.
The US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has approved new reporting rules for prediction markets as more companies look to enter the industry.
Under the new rules, announced on Monday, exchanges will report certain event contracts in a similar way as traditional futures and options trades. They will also no longer need to seek individual no-action relief from the CFTC for these reporting requirements.
The regulator said the rules will replace temporary reporting relief that exchanges have relied on for years. CFTC Chairman Michael Selig described the previous no-action letters as “band-aids for unworkable regulations.”
The new rules help to make it clearer how prediction markets should report their trading activity, especially as more companies look to enter the industry. As of September, the CFTC said in its final rule that it was reviewing at least 12 applications from companies looking to launch exchanges that could offer these types of contracts.
Notably, the rules apply to certain fully collateralized event contracts – meaning sufficient collateral must be set aside to cover any potential losses. New exchange operators will still need regulatory approval to launch.
Related: US Senate advances prediction market restrictions with DEATH BETS Act
Prediction market growth brings new reporting requirements
According to the CFTC’s final rule, exchanges certified about 1,600 event contracts for listing in 2025, compared with an average of just five new listings per year between 2006 and 2020.
While the CFTC expects the new rules to lower some reporting costs, exchanges will also be required to collect more information about their users, including names, addresses, occupations and employers.
The regulator added that knowing where traders work could help identify those who have access to inside information or could influence the outcome of an event. These concerns have also drawn attention from US lawmakers, who on Friday proposed rewarding whistleblowers with up to 30% of the financial penalties collected in certain prediction market fraud cases.
Exchanges will have one year from the rule’s publication in the Federal Register to meet the customer information requirements. Meanwhile, other changes will take effect in phases, with some deadlines occurring in 2027.
Related: CFTC staff say exchanges can count Bitcoin toward operating reserves
What else is happening?
The CFTC is also working on separate rules that could help clarify which events prediction markets can offer contracts on. The White House received the rules for review on Nov. 20, but the final text has not yet been made public.
On Nov. 19, the US Senate also passed the DEATH BETS Act, a bill that would ban federally regulated prediction markets from offering contracts tied to war, military operations, terrorism, assassinations and individual deaths. The bill is still awaiting House approval.
The latest reporting rules also do not resolve the ongoing legal battle between the CFTC and state gambling regulators over who should regulate prediction markets. The CFTC says that event contracts fall under its authority and has sued 12 states that argue sports-related contracts should be subject to state gambling laws.

articles.title: Bitcoin Losses Are the Worst Since FTX. Is the Bottom Near?
articles.text:
In brief
- Bitcoin’s realized losses relative to annual capital inflows are at their highest level since FTX collapsed in November 2022.
- U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs have lost $4.3 billion in net capital over the past 20 trading days.
- Glassnode says a close below $58,500 could open the way for Bitcoin to fall to its $53,200 realized price.
Bitcoin investors are locking in their heaviest losses since the collapse of FTX in November 2022, according to a report published Tuesday by blockchain analytics firm Glassnode.
The world’s largest cryptocurrency slipped below $60,000, trading at $59,992, more than 50% from its October 2025 peak.
“Bitcoin losses are the heaviest since FTX,” Glassnode wrote on X. “Set against the money that flowed into Bitcoin over the past year, they have almost doubled in a week.”
Did you know?
You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.
Glassnode tracks realized losses by looking at coins that move on-chain at prices lower than when they previously moved. Measuring those losses against the capital that entered Bitcoin over the preceding year gives analysts a way to compare sell-offs across market cycles, even as the cryptocurrency grows in value.
The last time the indicator reached these levels, Sam Bankman-Fried’s crypto empire was collapsing and Bitcoin was trading below $16,000. This time, the selling pressure has coincided with a much broader retreat from risky assets, and even good news for the tech industry hasn’t been enough to keep Bitcoin afloat.
Bitcoin rallied 5% in about half an hour on Monday after Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang was returning as CEO. Less than six hours later, Bitcoin had given back the entire rally, while the Nasdaq 100 still held roughly three-quarters of its gains. In trading, this is known as a bull trap, and happens on strong bearish trends.
Bitcoin’s correlation with the Nasdaq 100 is now at its highest since September 2022, Glassnode said. Over the past 60 trading days, Bitcoin has tended to gain less when tech stocks rise and lose more when they fall.
U.S. investors have also been pulling money out of the market. Spot Bitcoin ETFs have lost $4.3 billion on net over the past 20 trading days, while Coinbase traders have been heavy net sellers over the past month. Buying and selling on Binance, meanwhile, have been roughly balanced.
How much lower could Bitcoin go?
“Spikes like this often came close to past lows, but some came early,” Glassnode said. The firm pointed to the sell-offs of early 2019, March 2020, and November 2022, when losses surged near market bottoms, but also to earlier episodes in 2018 and 2022 when prices had further to fall.
Long-term holders—investors who have held their coins for roughly five months or longer—accounted for most realized losses from mid-April to mid-November. Nearly 90% of the long futures positions vulnerable to liquidation between last week’s Bitcoin price and $53,200 are also gone, reducing the potential for another cascade of forced selling within that range.
Glassnode is watching Bitcoin’s realized price, the average price at which circulating coins last moved, which currently stands at $53,200. Bitcoin traded below that metric before bottoming in each of the previous three major bear markets.
Applying the discounts seen at the lows of 2022 and 2018 to today’s realized price would put Bitcoin at roughly $41,000 and $37,000, respectively.
For now, the more immediate concern is whether Bitcoin can close above its June closing low of $58,500. Glassnode said a recovery above $60,000 accompanied by renewed ETF inflows would help establish whether the summer lows are holding.

articles.title: BlackRock Debuts Tokenized Fund in Hong Kong
articles.text:
BlackRock launches tokenized money market fund accepting stablecoins in Hong Kong
The tokenized fund launched with approximately $100 million in assets, with Standard Chartered and Ant International participating as seed investors.
Global asset manager BlackRock has launched its first tokenized money market fund in the Asia-Pacific region, allowing professional investors in Hong Kong to subscribe for and redeem shares using a locally issued stablecoins.
According to a Tuesday report by the South China Morning Post, the BlackRock HKD Digital Liquidity Fund launched with approximately $100 million in assets, with British banking group Standard Chartered and Ant International, a Singapore-based digital payments company spun out of China’s Ant Group, as seed investors.
The launch allows institutional investors to earn returns on their stablecoin holdings by investing directly in the fund, eliminating the need to convert their digital assets into traditional currency before investing.
The Hong Kong dollar, distinct from mainland China’s yuan, has been pegged to the US dollar since 1983.
Related: Hong Kong takes tokenized settlement to 24/7, plans stablecoin trials
BlackRock’s seed investors are also playing broader roles in the fund’s operations and adoption.
Subscriptions and redemptions can be carried out using HKDAP, a Hong Kong dollar-pegged stablecoin issued by Anchorpoint Financial, a joint venture between Standard Chartered, telecommunications company HKT and blockchain investment firm Animoca Brands. Standard Chartered also serves as the fund’s custodian, administrator, trustee and tokenization agent.
For Ant International, integrating the fund would support round-the-clock liquidity management across its global operations. According to the company’s disclosures, its payment services support more than 300 payment methods across 220 markets and process an average of over 20 million transactions daily.
BlackRock’s fund documentation shows that the fund began operations on Nov. 16, investing primarily in short-term securities issued or guaranteed by governments and high-grade bank deposits, with a net seven-day yield of 2.03% as of Tuesday. The fund may also accept tokenized deposits, while retail investors are limited to conventional Hong Kong dollars.
The fund’s launch follows HSBC’s Nov. 19 announcement that retail customers could invest in a tokenized money market fund using its Hong Kong dollar-backed stablecoin, RedCoin (RCHKD). HSBC and Anchorpoint Financial secured Hong Kong’s first two stablecoin issuer licenses in April, eight months after the city’s stablecoin regulatory framework took effect.

articles.title: What the CFTC’s New Crypto Reserves Guidance Actually Allows—And What It Doesn’t
articles.text:
In brief
- A CFTC staff advisory explains how swap execution facilities, exchanges and clearinghouses can use Bitcoin, Ethereum, and payment stablecoins to help meet their requirement to hold 12 months of operating costs in reserve, subject to volatility “haircuts.”
- The catch: crypto can’t count toward a separate liquidity requirement, because it doesn’t qualify as “cash” or “highly liquid securities” under GAAP—so firms still need traditional cash-like assets on hand.
- It’s the latest in the CFTC’s aggressive crypto push; the guidance is staff views only, not binding, and could shift as new commissioners arrive.
The U.S. derivatives regulator has quietly opened the door for crypto exchanges and clearinghouses to hold Bitcoin, Ethereum, and stablecoins as part of the financial cushion they’re required to keep, the latest sign of the agency weaving digital assets into the plumbing of regulated markets.
But the fine print matters, and it draws a careful line.
In a staff advisory issued this week, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission’s Division of Market Oversight and Division of Clearing and Risk explained how swap execution facilities, designated contract markets, and derivatives clearing organizations can use crypto assets to meet their financial-resources requirements.
Did you know?
You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.
Those rules require such platforms to hold enough resources to cover at least 12 months of operating costs, a buffer meant to ensure a venue can keep running or wind down safely if it hits trouble.
Here’s what the guidance allows: Certain crypto assets, specifically naming Bitcoin, Ethereum, and payment stablecoins, can now count toward that 12-month requirement, subject to “appropriate haircuts,” meaning their value would be discounted to account for volatility. That’s a meaningful concession, effectively recognizing crypto as a legitimate corporate reserve asset for the firms the CFTC oversees.
Here’s what it doesn’t allow, and this is the catch that defines the policy: Crypto can’t be counted toward a separate liquidity requirement.
Because digital assets don’t qualify as “cash” or “highly liquid securities” under Generally Accepted Accounting Principles, they fall short of that stricter test. In practice, a platform can hold Bitcoin or Ethereum as part of its longer-term financial backstop, but it still needs traditional cash-like instruments on hand to satisfy the rule meant to ensure it can pay obligations quickly.
The distinction is the whole point. It lets firms treat crypto as a store of value on their balance sheets while reinforcing that, when it comes to assets that must be instantly spendable, volatile tokens still don’t make the cut.
The nuance is easy to miss, but it reflects a measured posture from a regulator that has otherwise moved aggressively on crypto.
The CFTC has already previously cleared perpetual futures on individual stocks, issued no-action relief letting crypto apps offer regulated derivatives, and floated a plan to bring crypto exchanges under federal oversight, part of a broader push to set digital-asset policy on its own authority.
That said, it’s worth noting that the advisory represents the views of CFTC staff only. It creates no new rules or enforceable rights, isn’t a no-action position, and doesn’t necessarily reflect the views of the Commission itself.
It could also shift as the agency’s makeup changes. President Donald Trump recently sent a bipartisan slate of nominees to fill vacant CFTC and SEC seats, which could reshape the commissions now steering crypto policy.
For now, the guidance is best read not as crypto winning blanket acceptance as a reserve asset, but as the CFTC sorting out precisely where digital assets fit, and where they still don’t, in the machinery of regulated trading.

articles.title: South Korea Moves to Lift Its ICO Ban After Nearly a Decade
articles.text:
In brief
- South Korea’s Financial Services Commission proposed a draft bill to end its 2017 ICO ban, letting domestic projects issue and sell tokens for the first time in nearly a decade.
- Issuers and executives would face civil, financial and criminal liability for false disclosures.
- The ICO reversal is part of a broader overhaul also covering won-stablecoin rules and a 20% exchange-ownership cap.
South Korea is proposing to end its nine-year ban on initial coin offerings, a move aimed at pulling crypto fundraising back onshore, creating jobs and folding token sales into a regulated framework.
The country’s Financial Services Commission unveiled a draft bill, the Act on Digital Asset Industry Innovation and User Protection, on Tuesday that would reverse the prohibition imposed in September 2017, when regulators banned ICOs over fraud, speculation and investor losses.
If passed, it would let domestic projects issue and sell tokens to the public for the first time in nearly a decade.
Did you know?
You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.
Under the proposal, any issuer would have to file a “digital asset white paper” with the FSC before selling tokens, detailing the project, how the raised funds will be used, how many tokens will be issued and the risks involved. Issuers and their executives would face civil damages, financial penalties and possible criminal prosecution for false or omitted information, a liability regime modeled on the disclosure rules governing stock offerings.
The ban, regulators have concluded, never really worked. It largely pushed Korean projects to set up entities abroad and run their token sales through them, with game developers Wemade and Netmarble among the better-known firms that took the offshore route. The FSC’s stated goal is to reclaim that activity and the investment and jobs that went with it.
ETH price on November 29, 4:59PM UTC
The ICO reversal is one piece of a sweeping overhaul. The same bill would restrict issuance of Korean won-backed stablecoins to consortiums in which commercial banks hold a majority stake, cap any single major shareholder’s ownership of a crypto exchange at 20% (rising to 34% under certain conditions), extend market-manipulation rules to crypto-to-crypto trades, and organize the market into regulated verticals spanning exchanges, trading, brokerage, custody and asset management.
The shift fits a broader global move toward regulated token fundraising, as the U.S. and others build out frameworks that give crypto issuers clearer legal footing. It also marks a notable turn for South Korea, one of the world’s most active retail crypto markets, which has long paired enthusiastic trading with strict rules.
The proposal is only a draft. It now heads to the National Assembly, where lawmakers must approve it before any of the changes take effect, leaving the timeline, and the final shape of the rules, still to be determined.

articles.title: How South Korea’s Proposed 20% Cap Affects Naver’s Upbit Deal
articles.text:
How South Korea’s proposed 20% cap could change who runs Upbit
Naver Financial agreed to buy every share in Upbit’s operator, but a proposed ownership cap could strip away its voting rights on four-fifths of them.
When Naver struck its deal for Dunamu, the company behind crypto exchange Upbit, it had already worked out how to retain control of its financial arm.
Agreements with two Dunamu executives would give Naver 46.5% of the votes in Naver Financial despite owning just 17%. Control of Dunamu itself looked simpler, and Naver Financial would own it outright.
However, South Korea’s proposed ownership cap puts that second part of the deal in doubt. If lawmakers approve the bill, shares above the 20% cap would lose their votes.
Related: South Korea to permit crypto withdrawal freezes during hacking threats
With regulatory approval, a shareholder could vote up to 34%. The draft gives regulators no explicit power to order a sale, so Naver Financial could still hold every Dunamu share while losing the vote on most of them. That leaves investors in the $11.2 billion deal with a question the purchase price alone can’t answer.
Who would have the right to appoint the directors who oversee Upbit? The board and contractual rights Naver Financial retains could determine whether its parent can count Dunamu’s earnings in its accounts.

articles.title: Wall Street and Crypto Are in 'Extreme Fear'. What's Spooking Investors?
articles.text:
In brief
- Crypto market sentiment is back at its lowest levels since February, while Wall Street's Fear and Greed Index sits at 17 out of 100.
- Bitcoin has fallen below $60,000 again, with spot Bitcoin ETFs recording their worst month since launching in 2024.
- Concerns over AI spending, Nvidia's leadership crisis, and expectations of higher interest rates are weighing on investors.
Investors in both the stock and cryptocurrency markets are back in panic mode Tuesday, just one day after Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO triggered a massive rally across risk assets.
Bitcoin is trading at around $59,500, down 2.74% since the daily session opened, while the total cryptocurrency market capitalization has fallen 4.44% to $2.04 trillion, per CoinMarketCap. The Nasdaq and S&P 500 are also in the red, giving back some of Monday's gains.
CoinMarketCap's Fear and Greed Index (which tracks the sentiment across all the crypto market) currently sits at 9 out of 100, matching Friday's reading, the lowest since February. Just three months ago, the same indicator reached its yearly high of 82, corresponding to extreme greed.
Did you know?
You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.
Over on Wall Street, CNN's equivalent sits at 17, also in extreme fear territory, after reaching its lowest level since March on Friday.
Both indexes measure investor sentiment on a scale from zero to 100, with lower readings indicating greater fear. They use different methodologies, incorporating market momentum, volatility, and trading behavior rather than simply asking investors how they feel.
The AI trade is losing its appeal
The artificial intelligence industry, largely responsible for Wall Street's extraordinary performance over the past few years, is now at the center of the selloff.
Last week, the Nasdaq lost approximately 10%, its worst weekly performance since 2020, wiping out its gains for the year. The S&P 500 entered correction territory, having fallen more than 10% from its October peak.
Nvidia's leadership crisis made things considerably worse. The world's leading AI chipmaker had lost nearly half its market value from its October highs before the company's board reinstated Jensen Huang on Monday, sending its shares up 31.5% by the closing bell.
But having Huang back at Nvidia doesn't necessarily make AI investments more profitable.
Investors are increasingly questioning whether the hundreds of billions of dollars being spent on AI infrastructure will generate enough revenue to justify the expense. As Decrypt previously reported, 52% of respondents to Bank of America's November fund manager survey expect at least one major cloud computing company to announce spending cuts within six months.
Anthropic's much-anticipated IPO hasn't helped much, either. Shares of the Claude developer fell below their $83 offering price Tuesday, less than a week after the company made its stock market debut at $111.50.
Nvidia fell 5.8% during early trading Tuesday, while AI infrastructure providers CoreWeave and IREN lost 6.9% and 9%, respectively. Healthcare and consumer staples stocks were doing considerably better, suggesting investors are moving money into businesses less dependent on the AI boom.
The Fed isn't helping
An additional concern for both markets is that the U.S. Federal Reserve could make money more expensive at precisely the moment the AI industry needs more of it.
Traders are pricing in a 98% probability of a December interest rate hike and a 66% chance of another increase in January, according to CME FedWatch data.
Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for companies building data centers and reduce the present value of their expected future profits. They also make government bonds more attractive relative to speculative assets such as Bitcoin, which doesn't generate income for its holders.
For crypto investors, this comes at a particularly bad time.
U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded another $569.7 million in net withdrawals on Monday, despite Bitcoin's brief recovery, per Decrypt’s ETF tracker. BlackRock's IBIT alone accounted for $509.3 million.
November's cumulative Bitcoin ETF outflows have now reached $4.71 billion, surpassing June's previous monthly record with four trading sessions still remaining.
How much worse can things get for Bitcoin?
Bitcoin's daily chart shows a cryptocurrency struggling to hold a price range that has served as support on several occasions since 2024.
BTC has lost approximately 53% of its value from its October 2025 all-time high, and the recovery that took Bitcoin above $85,000 in September has largely evaporated.
The $60,000 area is particularly relevant because buyers stepped in around similar prices in February and June. Friday's dip toward $55,000 established another potential support area, with historical buying activity around $50,000 further below.
Extreme fear readings have historically coincided with some attractive buying opportunities, but they are notoriously unreliable at identifying the exact bottom. Bitcoin can remain oversold for extended periods, particularly when institutional investors are pulling billions of dollars out of the market.
Investors will get another important piece of economic data Wednesday, when the U.S. releases its Personal Consumption Expenditures inflation report, the Fed's preferred measure of inflation and the last major data release before its December monetary policy meeting.

articles.title: What Is Pons? The Robinhood Chain Meme Coin Launchpad Explained
articles.text:
In brief
- Pons is a non-custodial launchpad on Robinhood Chain that deploys fixed-supply tokens with locked liquidity; its own token, PONS, has a fixed supply of 1 billion.
- Its V2 contracts start each launch on a bonding curve with a decaying "snipe tax," which creators can waive for up to 32 wallets of their choosing.
- PONS was listed on Kraken in September 2026 and Coinbase in October 2026, as an analyst linked $18.43 million in extractions to a group using Pons V2.
When Robinhood switched on its own Robinhood Chain blockchain on July 1, 2026, the trading app's stock tokens were supposed to be the main attraction. Instead, much of the early activity came from meme coins: tokens built around a joke or an internet trend.
Pons became the busiest place to make them. Like Pump.fun on Solana, it lets anyone pick a name, ticker and image and have a tradable token minutes later, without writing code. Its fees briefly made it one of the highest-earning protocols in crypto, and its own token, PONS, went on to list on Kraken and Coinbase.
That openness can also be exploited. In September 2026, an onchain analyst alleged that one group had used Pons launches to extract millions of dollars from buyers.
This guide explains what Pons is, how its two generations of contracts work, what the PONS token does, and the risks.
What is Pons?
Pons is a token launch protocol running on Robinhood Chain, a layer-2 network built on Ethereum using Arbitrum's technology, and its website and documentation are published by Pons Labs, LLC.
Every token launched through Pons is a standard ERC-20 token with a fixed supply, 1 billion tokens on V1 launches, that can never be increased. The creator gets no allocation set aside before trading opens.
Pons is also non-custodial. Its documentation says every launch and trade is a transaction the user's own wallet signs, and the platform never holds user funds.
Pons went live within days of Robinhood Chain's mainnet. It picked up most of the chain's launchpad activity after an early rival, Noxa, stopped accepting new launches on July 11, 2026, according to Decrypt's reporting.
How does Pons work?
Pons has two generations of contracts, V1 and V2, and both remain live on Robinhood Chain.
Pons V1
In V1, a single transaction deploys the token and its trading pool, a Uniswap V3 pool paired with wrapped ETH (WETH), and locks the pool's liquidity so the creator can't withdraw it. Each launch costs 0.0005 ETH and carries a 1% trading fee, the documentation says. A launch "graduates" once 4.2 ETH has been paired in its pool by default, but trading carries on in the same pool.
V1 launches are protected for their first two blocks: in the launch block, only the creator's initial buy can execute, and for the rest of the window no wallet can hold more than 5% of supply or buy more than 5.5%. Fees are split 70% to the creator and 30% to the protocol for current launches.
Pons V2
V2 adds a bonding curve: a contract that holds a token's whole supply and sets its price by formula, rising as people buy and falling as they sell. According to the V2 documentation, the curve sells out, then "graduates" automatically into a Uniswap V4 pool, seeded with a fixed share of supply held back from the start. The pool's liquidity is then locked permanently; no unlock function exists.
V2 launches can be priced in ETH or in other assets Pons has approved, including tokenized stocks, in which case the creator is paid in that asset. Each trade pays a standard fee shared between Pons, the creator and an optional buyback, plus an optional creator tax that is capped by the protocol and fixed at launch.
When a creator turns buybacks on, part of their own fee is spent buying their token back. Those tokens are locked in a vault and released over five years, split between the creator and the protocol.
Did you know?
PONS itself was launched through Pons's own legacy V1 factory, and its documentation uses PONS as the reference token for developers testing their integrations.
Snipe protection and extraction allegations
"Sniping" means buying a large share of a new token in its first seconds, often with bots, then selling into later buyers. Every V2 launch opens with a "snipe tax" of 99% on buys that decays to zero over five seconds, the documentation says.
The launching wallet and the creator's fee wallet are exempt automatically, and creators can name up to 32 more exempt addresses at launch "for a team bundling its opening buys across several wallets."
That exemption became central to allegations published on September 27, 2026. Pseudonymous onchain analyst Wazz tweeted that a single operation had extracted at least $18.43 million from 53 Robinhood Chain launches between July 10 and September 21, 2026, mostly through Pons V2. Wazz said nearly every launch was sniped for 70% or more of its supply by bundles of 70 to 200 wallets.
I just uncovered the biggest serial Rugpulling and Extraction operation on Robinhood
The same operation is linked 53 launches within a 2 month period
Total Extracted: $18.43 MILLION
very likely more this is just what I could directly link
🧵 https://t.co/wS62KAbvv5 pic.twitter.com/BSxZL9wU44
— Wazz (@WazzCrypto) September 27, 2026
The Block reviewed the onchain data and found that creators of nine Pons V2 launches had exempted 15 to 25 wallets each from the snipe tax, which then bought out the bonding curve in a single transaction. The creator and those wallets held 82% to 86% of supply after the opening buys. The Block did not independently replicate Wazz's $18.43 million total.
What's so special about Pons?
On September 3, 2026, Pons generated $5.95 million in daily fees, briefly out-earning Robinhood Chain itself and ranking fourth among all protocols tracked by DefiLlama, Decrypt reported. Pons fees drove Robinhood Chain to a record of about $6 million in daily fees in early September 2026, The Block reported.
On September 5, 2026, blockchain analytics firm Arkham tweeted that crypto market maker Wintermute appeared to be buying PONS slowly in a series of small purchases, and held just over $3 million of the token. Wallets that Arkham attributes to Wintermute held about 3.4 million PONS at the time, and about 7.4 million as of November 2026.
As of November 20, 2026, DefiLlama put Pons's cumulative fees at about $205 million. Of that, $137 million came in September 2026 alone; fees fell to about $17 million in October 2026.
What is the PONS token?
PONS is the ERC-20 token tied to the Pons launchpad, with a fixed supply of 1 billion. Its link to the platform is a buyback.
According to the V1 documentation, 80% of the protocol's fees are used to buy PONS on the market through an automated process and send it to a burn address, permanently removing it from circulation. The remaining 20% pays for infrastructure and the Pons team. Kraken's listing notice describes the same mechanism.
As of November 20, 2026, CoinGecko data shows about 669 million PONS in circulation, out of a fixed supply of 1 billion.
You can track PONS's latest price on Decrypt's price page.
Where to buy PONS
PONS trades in Uniswap pools on Robinhood Chain. Binance Wallet added it to its Binance Alpha tier on September 2, 2026, and Kraken opened PONS trading on September 25, 2026, with access through the Kraken App and Instant Buy to follow once liquidity allows. Coinbase Markets tweeted on October 6, 2026, that it had added PONS to its listing roadmap, and said the next day that its PONS-USD pair would open later that day, if liquidity conditions were met.
The future of Pons
Pons has flagged several changes still to come. Its V1 documentation says the 80% share of protocol fees used to buy back PONS is not yet fixed in its contracts, but will become "immutable, decentralized, and automated" in a future release.
On V2, three security firms (SB Security, Dingbats and Pashov Audit Group) are reviewing the contracts, and Pons says it will publish their reports in full, including any findings it did not accept, once the reviews close. Until then, its documentation tells users to treat V2 as unaudited, and only whitelisted addresses can create V2 tokens.
Pons also faces competition on its home chain. Uniswap, already Robinhood Chain's main exchange, launched its own launchpad, Pools.trade, on August 5, 2026. It charges no launchpad fee, locks each launch's liquidity permanently, and offers a "crowd launch" option designed to resist bundling. Within its first days, Pools.trade took about half of Robinhood Chain's launchpad volume, Decrypt's Morning Minute newsletter reported. The newsletter noted that Uniswap can afford to forgo launchpad fees because it earns from its other products, which most dedicated launchpads cannot.
Pons has since kept the larger share of fees. As of November 2026, DefiLlama showed Pons collecting about $5.6 million in fees over the previous 30 days, against about $115,000 for Pools.trade. The two charge different rates, though: Pools.trade's trading fee is 0.25%, while Pons's standard fee is 1%.
V2's tokenized-stock pairs link Pons launches to the stock tokens Robinhood built the chain to carry, which ties Pons's prospects to Robinhood Chain itself. On Robinhood's third-quarter earnings call on October 27, 2026, CEO Vlad Tenev said the growth of the chain and its ecosystem had exceeded the company's expectations, and that Robinhood was investing in how to support the chain's developer community.
